summary: At Passover Jesus drives the merchants and money changers out of the temple and, asked for a sign, points to the temple of His body.
key_insight: When the leaders demanded a sign, Jesus gave one: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” No one understood it, not even His disciples, until after the resurrection. The true meeting place of God and people was His body.
story: The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

In the temple He found people selling oxen, sheep and doves, and money changers doing business at their tables. He made a whip of cords and drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the oxen. He poured out the changers’ money and overturned the tables.
To those who sold doves He said, “Take these things away! Do not make My Father’s house a house of merchandise!” His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for Your house has eaten Me up.”
The Jews there responded, “What sign do You show to us, since You do these things?” Jesus answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
They said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will You raise it up in three days?” But He was speaking of the temple of His body.
After He had risen from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word Jesus had spoken.

fit.question: John places this cleansing at the first Passover of Jesus’ ministry. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of Jesus clearing the temple in His last week (event 134). Did He do it twice, or is this one event placed differently?

points.label: Two cleansings
points.text: Many scholars, McGarvey among them, hold that Jesus cleared the temple twice, at the start and at the end of His ministry. The details differ: here a whip, sheep and oxen, “a house of merchandise,” and a saying about His body; later, the words of Isaiah and Jeremiah, “a house of prayer for all nations” and “a den of thieves.” John ties his account to the “forty-six years” of building, which fits the early years. And at Jesus’ trial witnesses garbled the saying about destroying the temple (Mark 14:58), which fits a saying spoken years before.

points.label: One cleansing, placed for its meaning
points.text: Others hold that there was one cleansing. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of only one visit to Jerusalem during Jesus’ ministry, so they would naturally place it there; or John set it at the start because it shows what Jesus’ whole ministry means. Those who hold this view doubt that the temple authorities would have allowed such an act twice.

fit.note: Faithful scholars land in different places. The two-cleansing view takes every note of time at face value; the one-cleansing view holds that a writer may arrange events by theme without claiming exact order. Neither requires an error.
fit.short: Many think Jesus cleared the temple twice, at the start and end of His ministry; others think one cleansing is placed differently. Views differ.

scene.label: The temple market
scene.text: Pilgrims needed animals without blemish for their sacrifices, and buying them in Jerusalem saved a long journey with livestock. But this trade was set up inside the temple courts, probably in the outer Court of the Gentiles, the only place where non-Jews could come to pray.

scene.label: Money changers
scene.text: Every Jewish man paid a yearly temple tax of a half-shekel (Exodus 30:13). It had to be paid in a particular silver coin, usually the shekel of Tyre, so changers swapped pilgrims’ coins for a fee.

scene.label: Forty-six years
scene.text: Herod began rebuilding the temple about 20/19 BC. Forty-six years later points to about AD 27/28, the first Passover of Jesus’ ministry. The work went on for decades more and was finished only a few years before the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

scene.label: “Zeal for Your house”
scene.text: The disciples remembered Psalm 69:9. It is a psalm of a righteous man who suffers for God’s sake, and the New Testament quotes it again of Jesus’ sufferings. Zeal for God’s house would one day cost Jesus His life.

witnesses.john: John places this cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry, at the first of several Passovers he mentions (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is how we know the ministry lasted more than two years. He alone records the saying about the temple of His body and the disciples’ remembering after the resurrection, the view of a witness looking back after Easter.

seeing.reveals: Jesus acts with the authority of a Son in His Father’s house. He burns with zeal for true worship, and He Himself is the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days.
seeing.living: Jesus was not against the temple; He was against what had been made of it. Worship turned into business, and religion used for gain, still stir His zeal. Ask Him to clear out whatever crowds out prayer in your life and your church, and come to God through Jesus, the true temple.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus walked into your place of worship, or into your heart, what tables would He overturn?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus cleanses His Father’s house and offers Himself as the true temple.
outline: The sign of the true temple (19–21)
preaching.watch_for: Twice John says the disciples “remembered” (2:17, 22). Some things about Jesus become clear only in the light of the resurrection, and John writes as one who remembered.
